moments.title: China rejected to an AI slowdown. So did the US government. A clear No to Dario's proposal. Reuters reports that Global Times accused the US of trying “to curb China’s AI development through technological barriers and re
moments.selftext: China rejected to an AI slowdown. So did the US government. A clear No to Dario's proposal. Reuters reports that Global Times accused the US of trying “to curb China’s AI development through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies.” It called the proposal a “silent AI Cold War” that is “hypocritical and short-sighted.” China’s Foreign Ministry used more diplomatic language. According to AP: “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance which serves no one’s interest.” Beijing’s position is clear: it supports international AI governance, but rejects a slowdown combined with US restrictions on Chinese compute and model development. Slow down is over friends before it even started.

moments.title: “An enemy will agree, but a friend will argue.” - Russian Proverb The Russian proverb “An enemy will agree, but a friend will argue” reflects a traditional belief that genuine friendship requires honesty rather than cons
moments.selftext: “An enemy will agree, but a friend will argue.” - Russian Proverb The Russian proverb “An enemy will agree, but a friend will argue” reflects a traditional belief that genuine friendship requires honesty rather than constant approval. Russian proverbial wisdom often emphasizes loyalty, truthfulness, and the value of sincere criticism between people who care about one another. The saying suggests that an enemy may agree simply to avoid conflict, deceive, or allow someone to make a mistake. A true friend, however, is willing to disagree and challenge poor decisions, making honest arguments a sign of genuine concern and friendship.

moments.title: Weird Al Yankovic doesn't need permission (under US copyright law) to make a parody of someone's song. “Weird Al” Yankovic built his career by transforming popular songs into comedic parodies, beginning with early record
moments.selftext: Weird Al Yankovic doesn't need permission (under US copyright law) to make a parody of someone's song. “Weird Al” Yankovic built his career by transforming popular songs into comedic parodies, beginning with early recordings in the late 1970s. Under U.S. copyright law, qualifying parodies can be protected as fair use, meaning permission from the original artist is not necessarily required. Despite this legal protection, Yankovic has long followed a personal policy of asking artists for permission before releasing parodies. This approach has helped him maintain good relationships within the music industry, even though some artists have occasionally declined his requests.
